title: Appendix C: Security, Privacy, and Cost Review

sections.title: Tests That Attempt a Forbidden Action
Privacy and the Life of Personal Data

html:
A design can meet its latency objective, recover after a dependency failure, and still be unsuitable for production. An employee may be able to retrieve another merchant’s orders. A deleted customer’s details may survive in a search index or training dataset. A new assistant may serve every request successfully while its model usage costs more than the product can afford.

These problems are easy to miss when the review concentrates on databases, queues, and instance counts. They deserve the same questions we have asked throughout the book. Which operation is permitted? Where does its data go? What resources does it consume? What evidence would show that the current design is unsafe or too expensive?

This appendix provides a short review that can accompany the architectural and recovery reviews in the main chapters. It identifies engineering evidence to collect and decisions that need an owner. Specific legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations should be confirmed with the people responsible for them rather than inferred from an architecture diagram.

Security

Consider a merchant employee who may view an order but is not permitted to refund it. The employee signs in successfully, retrieves an order, and changes the HTTP request to call the refund endpoint. Authentication has established the employee’s identity. The refund service still needs to establish whether that employee may refund this particular payment, for this merchant, in the requested amount.

That check belongs at the service responsible for the operation. A gateway can reject unauthenticated requests and apply broad access policy, but resource ownership and the current business state may be known only by the owning service. A well-formed order ID or a valid access token does not establish permission for every record the caller can name.

Identity, Resource, and Action

For each protected API, Baodium recorded three facts: the authenticated principal, the resource being accessed, and the requested action. It also recorded the policy inputs needed to decide permission, such as merchant membership, payment state, refund amount, and approval expiry.

Roles and token scopes can grant broad capabilities such as orders:read or refunds:create. The service may still need a relationship check to establish which merchant’s records the principal can access. Role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC) can coexist in one application. A separate policy engine becomes useful when several services need a common, independently managed policy, with a defined availability and revocation contract.

Calls between services require their own authentication and authorization. A network address or the fact that a request originated inside the cluster is insufficient. The receiving service verifies a workload identity and its permitted operation. If it acts on a customer’s behalf, it also needs trustworthy evidence of the delegated customer identity and the scope of that authority. Chapter 4 examined those call chains, while Chapter 11 applied the same rules to merchant-scoped data.

Asynchronous work needs a time rule. An employee may approve a refund at 09:00, but the worker may not execute it until 09:30. The review must state whether the approval can expire or be revoked before dispatch, and which component checks it. Deployment authorization has the same problem. The approved image digest, configuration, environment, and current policy must match the protected action when the deployment controller grants execution, as Chapter 10 established.

Failures and Privileged Operations

The engineers also examined what happens when a security dependency is unavailable. If a payment refund requires a current permission decision, a timeout from the policy service cannot become an approval. The caller returns a refusal or an explicitly pending outcome under the business contract. An optional feature flag or a low-risk read may use a different fallback, but that choice must be documented and tested. Rate-limit failure policies also need to reflect what the limit protects. A failed login-abuse limiter has different consequences from a failed allocation for optional image thumbnails.

Service credentials were reviewed for the damage they could cause if compromised. A notification worker should not have permission to modify payment records, and a catalog reader should not have unrestricted access to the merchant database. The team tested secret rotation and credential revocation rather than assuming that a short-lived token would solve long-running sessions or cached credentials. Secrets and access tokens were excluded from ordinary logs and model prompts.

The software supply chain was part of this boundary. Builds recorded their source revision, dependency versions, base image, and published artifact digest. Release roles controlled who could replace an artifact or approve its deployment. Recovery utilities deserved similar restrictions. A manual payment override, event replay, or emergency admission increase could change production state, so each action required an authenticated operator, permitted scope, and an audit record. Appendix A describes the evidence needed to investigate those changes later.

Tests That Attempt a Forbidden Action

A successful sign-in test tells us little about resource authorization. Baodium included negative tests alongside normal API and recovery tests.

These tests check the boundary that performs the action. A gateway rule alone cannot protect a service that accepts unauthorized internal calls. Denials also need useful telemetry, with confidential identifiers kept in access-controlled records rather than high-cardinality metric labels.

Privacy and the Life of Personal Data

A customer’s email address may enter through an account API and then be copied into a cache, search index, event, log, analytics table, feature store, and backup. The primary account database may be the only place shown on the first architecture diagram. A deletion or access restriction will be incomplete if the team does not know where those other copies are stored.

Baodium’s data review followed a representative personal-data field through collection, processing, replication, export, and deletion. For each destination, the record named the purpose, owner, access policy, retention interval, and region or external processor involved. That inventory included logs and traces, where request payloads and tokens can be recorded unintentionally, and the model inputs from Chapter 13, where an external inference provider may receive the contents of a prompt.

A first design can reduce many problems by collecting less data. If a service needs an order reference and delivery region, it should not copy the full customer profile into every event. Analytical consumers may need an opaque customer key rather than an email address. The team checked whether access to raw values was necessary and whether the same result could be produced from a narrower representation.

Deletion, Derived Records, and Restore

Deletion becomes difficult once data has been copied. Catalog projections from Chapter 11, retained events from Chapter 12, and feature histories and training datasets from Chapter 13 each need a documented treatment for deletion or correction. Some stores can remove a record directly. Others need a tombstone, an index rebuild, a new dataset version, or a scheduled retention process. The applicable policy determines whether and how these techniques satisfy the underlying obligation.

Baodium treated a deletion request as a tracked workflow. The request identified the affected person and permitted scope. Each responsible system recorded its completion or an exception requiring review. A successful deletion response depended on the agreed completion rule, rather than the account database’s row count alone. An event consumer that was offline when the deletion event appeared needed a durable catch-up or reconciliation path.

Backups create a separate case. A backup taken before deletion can contain personal data that is absent from the live database. Its permitted retention and access restrictions must be reviewed with the legal and privacy owners. If the backup is restored, deletion and restriction records applied after the backup’s snapshot need to be replayed or reconciled before the restored service exposes that data. A restore test that verifies database availability without checking those records is incomplete.

The European launch from Chapter 14 also introduced location and transfer questions. A data-residency or processing restriction can apply to replicas, backups, analytics, support access, and external model providers, not just the primary database. The team documented the actual data paths and checked the applicable jurisdictional and contractual requirements before enabling another region or provider.

Cost

A system may meet its response and recovery objectives at a cost the product cannot sustain. That matters especially when a single customer request generates several dependency calls, background jobs, or model invocations. Cost per API request can conceal an expensive operation that starts before the response and finishes much later.

The useful starting measure is the cost of a completed customer outcome. The team includes retries, refused and incomplete requests, shared infrastructure, replication, recovery capacity, and delayed processing where they contribute to that outcome. Estimates should identify which costs are fixed, which grow with usage, and which depend on a provider’s pricing or quota contract.

A Model-Serving Cost Example

Consider an assistant handling 10 million customer interactions per day. For this example, each interaction generates 1.4 model calls on average, and every call uses 1,200 input tokens and 300 output tokens. Assume hypothetical rates of $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. These are calculation inputs, not a quotation from a provider.

Input per call=1,200×$3106=$0.0036,Output per call=300×$15106=$0.0045,Total per call=$0.0081,Daily model cost=107×1.4×$0.0081=$113,400.\begin{align*} \text{Input per call} &= 1{,}200 \times \frac{\$3}{10^6} = \$0.0036,\\ \text{Output per call} &= 300 \times \frac{\$15}{10^6} = \$0.0045,\\ \text{Total per call} &= \$0.0081,\\ \text{Daily model cost} &= 10^7 \times 1.4 \times \$0.0081\\ &= \$113{,}400. \end{align*}Input per callOutput per callTotal per callDaily model cost​=1,200×106$3​=$0.0036,=300×106$15​=$0.0045,=$0.0081,=107×1.4×$0.0081=$113,400.​

The model calls alone cost about $113,400 a day under those assumptions. Reducing every prompt by 25 percent saves 300 input tokens per call, or $12,600 a day at the stated volume. An additional ten percent in model calls costs $11,340 a day if the average tokens per call remain the same.

Real assistant loops often violate that last assumption. Later calls may include accumulated tool results and conversation history, so their prompts can be longer than the first one. Prefix caching, different output lengths, failed requests, and provider-specific billing rules also change the bill. Baodium recorded actual input and output token use by interaction outcome and tracked the average and upper tail of cost per completed task. The same review included tool APIs, data transfer, retrieval storage, and any self-managed inference capacity.

Telemetry and Reserved Capacity

Telemetry has a separate scaling risk. A metric labeled by twelve endpoints, five status classes, and two hundred instances can produce 12,000 time series. Adding a customer-ID label with two million possible values creates a theoretical cross-product of 2.4×10102.4\times10^{10}2.4×1010 combinations. The actual number observed may be smaller, but an unbounded customer dimension can make monitoring costly and queries impractical. Individual operation and customer identities belong in suitably protected traces and records, with bounded metric labels for aggregate monitoring.

The design also pays for capacity that cannot be allocated to every new request. Chapter 14 reserved 45 of the 200 concurrent payment calls for captures, reconciliation, and emergency recovery. That is 22.5 percent of the operating allocation protected from new authorizations. The capacity may be used routinely for its assigned classes, although it cannot be borrowed freely to increase authorization throughput. The review needs to account for that tradeoff before estimating customer capacity or describing unused permits as waste.

Costs should be revisited at twice the forecast traffic and during a failure. A cache outage can multiply database reads. Retries can add provider charges while completion falls. A delayed analytics consumer can create an expensive replay after the primary incident is over. The cost model and the recovery test should use the same workload and admission assumptions wherever possible.

A One-Page Review

Table Table collects the questions that tend to change an architectural decision. The reviewer records the owner, supporting evidence, and unresolved action beside the design, rather than assuming that every answer is complete because the diagram has been approved.

The security review establishes who can perform an operation. The privacy review follows the data that operation creates or exposes. The cost review establishes whether the work and its recovery can be sustained. Together they add constraints that a design must satisfy before its performance measurements alone can justify deployment.
